quote_orig: Perhaps the most striking example of this is the massive four-volume, 3,600-page Handbook for the Study of the Historical Jesus (2011), which contains no discussion of whether the historical Jesus ever made divine claims. The implication of such a gaping lacuna is clear: it is so self-evident that Jesus did not claim to be divine that the topic is not even worthy of discussion. For contemporary Jesus research taken as a whole, the answer to the question, "Did Jesus claim to be divine?," is a resounding no.
context_before: Pitre: "...one searches most major monographs on the historical Jesus in vain for any mention of the possibility that Jesus may have made divine claims during his lifetime." He then cites the Handbook. The sentences before this in the article describe the view he is rejecting; he concludes (see notes) that "a strong case can be made that the historical Jesus claimed to be divine."
what_it_says: Pitre states that contemporary Jesus research as a whole answers "no" to whether Jesus claimed to be divine, and he cites the Handbook as an example of silence on the question.
claim_supported: (E) other: a scholarly-consensus description that Pitre attributes to others and rejects
scholar_qualification: Pitre does not hold the view; it is his summary of the view he disputes. The same article concludes that "the best explanation for why the earliest Jewish followers of Jesus believed he was divine shortly after his death is because Jesus himself spoke and acted as if he were divine during his lifetime" (Church Life Journal). Using the sentence as a concession by Pitre would misstate his position. The Handbook claim is contradicted by Pitre's own footnote 26 (see J10-02).
source_type: other (Church Life Journal, University of Notre Dame; excerpt reprinted by permission of Eerdmans)
limits: Read verbatim in two copies (Church Life Journal HTML and Substack reprint; the wording matches). Book page not shown; the book itself was not read. The video's version is dated "about Feb 2024"; the article is dated 4 Feb 2025.

quote_orig: If Jesus went around Galilee proclaiming himself to be a divine being sent from God—one who existed before the creation of the world, who was in fact equal with God—could anything else that he might say be so breathtaking and thunderously important? And yet none of these earlier sources [i.e., the Synoptic material] says any such thing about him. page: page unknown (Gutenberg text has no printed pagination); Pitre's 1935 Watts citation: p. 132
quote_orig: That Jesus never dreamt of making himself pass for an incarnation of God, is a matter about which there can be no doubt. Such an idea was entirely foreign to the Jewish mind; and there is no trace of it in the synoptical gospels,[1] we only find it indicated in portions of the Gospel of John, which cannot be accepted as expressing the thoughts of Jesus.
context_before: Chapter XV opens: "Jesus returned to Galilee, having completely lost his Jewish faith, and filled with revolutionary ardor."
what_it_says: Renan says Jesus never presented himself as an incarnation of God, that no trace of this is in the Synoptics, and that it appears only in portions of John.

The video's sentence ("leaves no trace ... appears only in some passages of John") is a close paraphrase, not a verbatim Renan sentence, and it is not from Vermes.
